answer.evidence: The object is a tiny cluster of rocks spanning rows 6-13 and up to 12 px wide. Each column scan shows the same sequence: a darker top pixel, one lighter highlight row (x=7 row 7, x=10 row 11), a mid-tone row, a darker row, and then a near-black outline row (L=27). The highlight is a single row, so it is a rim and not a top plane. There is no ellipse, no front-edge line followed by eave shadow, and no open contents. The silhouette is a lumpy mound with 3-4 rows of vertical face under the highlight, so no horizontal top surface of 3 or more rows can be pointed at.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny cluster of grey basalt rocks, well under one 16x16 tile (about 14x10 px), next to two large trees with canopy and trunk. The kind does not match well: these are rocks, not a plant, so the reference comparison is only approximate. The measured tones per tile are 0 because the piece is smaller than a tile, so I judged by eye. It has only 10 distinct colours and about 3 visible grey steps (light top, mid, dark base). The shading looks shallow. The rocks read as a few blobs with little stone-by-stone shading, grain or highlight clusters, unlike the references' multi-tone leaf clumps and bark texture. Only 6% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is mostly tinted rather than a pure black line, but at this size it is hard to call it a deliberate dark-material-tone outline. It is clearly thinner and simpler than either reference at the same scale. A careful artist would not accept it next to the references without it looking thinner and flatter.
